synapses.text: Every language here compiles or interprets down to the same machines; what differs is what each one makes easy, safe or fast to express.
Functional, object-oriented and concurrent styles are ways of organising the same problems; most modern languages borrow from all three.
Quicksort and Dijkstra are older than almost every language in use; data structures and complexity are the durable part of the craft.
Memory, compilers, operating systems and networks shape what a program can do; the best abstractions still leak at the edges.

synapses.lead: Craft is what makes code last
synapses.text: Version control, tests, review and documentation are the difference between a program and software.
Lovelace, Turing, Hopper, Dijkstra, Knuth, Liskov, Ritchie and Thompson each appear in several other neurons of this brain.
Guido van Rossum began Python at CWI in the Netherlands in the late 1980s; version 0.9.0 was released in February 1991 and Python 2 and 3 followed in 2000 and 2008.
PEP 20 lists the guiding aphorisms: "Beautiful is better than ugly", "Explicit is better than implicit", "There should be one obvious way to do it".
Blocks are delimited by indentation rather than braces, which makes the visual structure and the actual structure the same thing.

synapses.lead: Reference counting plus a cycle collector
synapses.text: CPython frees most objects the instant their reference count hits zero and runs a separate collector for reference cycles.
The built-in sort is Timsort, written by Tim Peters for Python 2.3 in 2002; it exploits runs that are already ordered.

synapses.lead: One lock to rule the bytecode
synapses.text: The GIL simplifies memory management in the interpreter and keeps C extensions safe, at the cost of true multi-core parallelism for pure-Python threads.
Accepted in 2023, PEP 703 made a GIL-free build of CPython available as an experimental option starting with Python 3.13 in 2024.
multiprocessing, C extensions that release the GIL, and asyncio for I/O-bound work are the long-standing ways around the lock.
CPython is developed in the open at python/cpython; the GitHub migration from Mercurial completed in 2017.
Type hints standardised annotation syntax and the typing module; the interpreter does not enforce them.
You can annotate one function at a time, which is what made adoption in large codebases possible.
list[int], TypeVar and Protocol (PEP 544) give Python parametric and structural typing in the checker.
Brendan Eich wrote the first version at Netscape in 1995; the name was a marketing nod to Java, to which it is unrelated.
Ecma International published ECMA-262 in 1997; ES2015 (ES6) added classes, modules, arrow functions, promises and let/const, and editions have shipped yearly since.
JavaScript runs one thread per realm; asynchronous work is queued as callbacks, promises and microtasks on the event loop.
Objects inherit from other objects via a prototype chain; the class keyword (ES2015) is syntax over the same mechanism.
Valid JavaScript is valid TypeScript; the compiler checks types and then erases them, emitting JavaScript.
Two types are compatible when their shapes match, regardless of their names; this is what lets TypeScript describe existing JavaScript APIs.
TypeScript has been developed publicly at microsoft/TypeScript since its 2012 announcement.
Node embeds Chrome's V8 engine and adds a libuv-based event loop, file system and networking APIs.
npm, released in 2010, became the largest package registry; the 2016 left-pad removal showed how deep the dependency chains ran.
Node is developed at nodejs/node under the OpenJS Foundation.
Promise reactions go on the microtask queue, which drains completely before the next macrotask (timers, I/O callbacks) runs.
The callback waits for the current stack and all pending microtasks; zero is a minimum, not a promise.
Rust frees memory deterministically when an owner goes out of scope; the compiler rejects programs that could use freed or aliased-and-mutated memory.
The same ownership rules that prevent use-after-free also prevent data races at compile time.
Linux 6.1 (December 2022) merged initial infrastructure for writing kernel modules in Rust.
Errors and absence are values, not exceptions or null; the ? operator propagates them.
The compiler and standard library live at rust-lang/rust.
Assigning a non-Copy value moves it; using the old binding afterwards is a compile error.
At any point you may have any number of &T or exactly one &mut T; this rule is what rules out data races and iterator invalidation.
Lifetime annotations tell the compiler how long references must be valid; most are inferred by elision rules.

synapses.lead: One tool for build, test, docs
synapses.text: cargo build, cargo test, cargo doc and cargo publish cover the whole workflow; the uniformity is part of why the ecosystem feels coherent.
Cargo.lock records resolved versions so a fresh checkout builds the same graph.
Go was a reaction to slow builds and complexity at Google: fast compilation, a small language, one standard formatter.
Type parameters landed in Go 1.18 (March 2022) after a decade of proposals.
The formatter is part of the toolchain and the community norm; style arguments mostly ended.
The toolchain and standard library are at golang/go.
A goroutine starts with a small stack that grows as needed, so programs routinely run thousands at once.
Channels carry values between goroutines; select waits on several channel operations at once.
Rob Pike's 2012 talk of that title separates structuring a program as independent parts from running them simultaneously.
C grew out of B and BCPL so that Unix could be portable; the 1978 Kernighan and Ritchie book defined the language for a generation.
ANSI C (1989) was followed by C99, C11, C17 and C23, each adding features while keeping old code compiling.
C exposes memory directly: arrays decay to pointers, structs have layouts, and malloc/free are your responsibility.
Almost every language can call C, so C headers are how libraries and operating systems talk to each other.
&x yields the address of x; *p reads or writes what p points at; p + 1 advances by one element, not one byte.
Use-after-free, double free, buffer overflow and null dereference are all pointer misuse; Rust's ownership model was designed to make them compile errors.
UB lets the compiler assume programs are well-formed; the cost is that a single overflow can make an optimiser delete a bounds check.
AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer instrument builds to report UB as it happens.
Functions have no side effects and expressions are evaluated only when needed, which allows infinite data structures and demands a different intuition about performance.
Ad-hoc polymorphism via type classes (1989, Wadler and Blott) influenced Rust traits and Swift protocols.
IO, Maybe and State are monads: a common interface for sequencing computations with context.
Programs are lists, so macros can transform code before it runs; this homoiconicity is Lisp's defining feature.

synapses.lead: Garbage collection was invented for Lisp
synapses.text: McCarthy described automatic reclamation of list cells in 1959.
Proper tail-call optimisation is required by the Scheme standard, so loops are written as recursion.
A query describes the result set; the planner decides joins, indexes and order.
Relations, tuples and attributes come from E. F. Codd's 1970 paper; SQL is one (imperfect) syntax for them.
Standard SQL exists, but PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and SQL Server each differ in types, functions and quoting.
Church's calculus of function abstraction and application (1930s) is Turing-complete and the theoretical basis of functional languages.

synapses.lead: Pure functions are easy to test
synapses.text: Same inputs, same output, no side effects: pure functions can be tested, memoised and parallelised without ceremony.
map/filter/reduce, lambdas and immutable collections are in Python, JavaScript, Java, Rust and C#; FP won by diffusion.
Structural sharing lets an "updated" tree reuse most of the old one, so immutability is not a copy of everything every time.
If nothing mutates, there is nothing to race on; immutability is the simplest concurrency strategy.
The three operations cover most list processing and are the gateway to thinking in transformations instead of loops.
A function returned from another keeps access to the variables it was created with; this is how callbacks and decorators carry state.
Simula 67 had classes and inheritance; Smalltalk (1970s) made everything an object and message passing the core idea.
Kay later said the big idea was messaging and late binding, not classes and inheritance.
Code written against an interface works with any implementation; the Liskov substitution principle says when that is safe.
Barbara Liskov's 1987 keynote: a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is, without breaking the program.
Depend on abstractions, not concretions; it is what makes code testable with fakes and mocks.

synapses.lead: The Gang of Four said it first
synapses.text: Design Patterns (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994) lists "favor object composition over class inheritance" as a principle.
Rust traits, Go interfaces and TypeScript structural types all push toward composition.
Static checking happens before running (Rust, Go, TypeScript); dynamic checking at runtime (Python, JavaScript); gradual systems mix them.
Tony Hoare called null references his "billion-dollar mistake" in a 2009 talk; Option types are the remedy.
A signature tells you what a function needs and promises; tooling turns that into completion, refactoring and errors at edit time.
List<T> or Vec<T> is written once; the type parameter is filled at each use and checked statically.
Constraints such as T: Ord or comparable say what the generic code is allowed to do with T.
A struct is a product (all fields); an enum is a sum (one of several variants); together they describe most data shapes.
Maybe/Option replaces null and Either/Result replaces exceptions; the compiler forces every case to be handled.
A decidable algorithm that infers the most general type of an expression without annotations; the foundation of ML-family type systems.
let x = 5 or const x = [] infers from the right-hand side; function signatures are still written out for readability and error quality.
Concurrency is about structure (many things in flight); parallelism about execution (many things at once). You can have either without the other.
Speed-up is limited by the serial fraction of a program; eight cores do not make an 80 percent-serial program eight times faster.
Shared memory with locks, message passing, async tasks on one thread, or actors: each language leans toward one.
An async task runs until it awaits; the scheduler then runs another. One slow synchronous call blocks everyone.
Async functions can only be awaited from async functions, which splits a codebase in two; the 2015 essay "What Color is Your Function?" named the problem.
Actors cannot read each other's memory, so there is nothing to lock; failures are isolated and supervised.
Erlang (Ericsson, 1986) runs millions of lightweight processes and restarts failed ones from supervisors rather than defending against every error.
Dijkstra introduced semaphores in the 1960s; mutexes are the binary case and remain the basic tool for protecting shared state.
Two threads each holding a lock the other needs; consistent lock ordering or avoiding nested locks prevents it.
Rust's Send and Sync traits turn most data races into type errors; sanitizers find them at runtime elsewhere.
The notation comes from number theory (Bachmann 1894, Landau 1909); Knuth standardised its use in algorithm analysis.
Quicksort is O(n²) worst case but O(n log n) on average; a dynamic array's append is O(1) amortised over many pushes.
An O(n) scan of a small array often beats an O(log n) tree because of caches and branch prediction.
Two keys can hash to one bucket; chaining stores a list per bucket, open addressing probes for the next free slot.
When the table fills past a threshold it doubles and rehashes; that occasional O(n) step is why append is amortised O(1).
Python dicts (insertion-ordered since 3.7) and JavaScript Maps are hash tables; Rust's HashMap uses a DoS-resistant SipHash by default.
A binary search tree degrades to a linked list if inserts arrive sorted; AVL (1962) and red-black trees rebalance to keep O(log n).
File systems, DOM, parse trees, JSON documents and Git commit graphs are trees or near-trees.
Walking left, node, right visits keys in ascending order, which makes BSTs a natural ordered map.
C++ std::map and Java TreeMap are red-black trees; Rust's BTreeMap is, as the name says, a B-tree.
Each node fills a page and holds hundreds of keys, so a lookup touches only a handful of pages even for billions of rows.
Both store tables and indexes as B-tree variants; the SQLite file format documentation describes its B+-tree pages in detail.
Keys with common prefixes share paths, so a trie of a dictionary is compact and prefix queries are a walk, not a search.
Compressed tries (radix/Patricia trees) are used for IP longest-prefix matching in routers.
Lists suit sparse graphs (most real ones); matrices suit dense graphs and constant-time edge checks.
Breadth-first search finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search underlies cycle detection and topological sort.
The layout you are looking at treats pages as charged particles and links as springs; it is a graph algorithm too.
Dijkstra said he worked it out over coffee in Amsterdam in 1956 to demonstrate a new computer; it was published in 1959.
A negative edge can make an already-settled node wrong; Bellman–Ford handles negatives at higher cost.
A* (1968) is Dijkstra with an admissible estimate of remaining distance, which is what game and map routing use.
Repeatedly remove nodes with no incoming edges (Kahn, 1962), or reverse the finish order of a depth-first search.
If a cycle exists there is no valid order, which is how package managers detect circular dependencies.
Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; counting and radix sorts sidestep it by not comparing.
A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order, which matters when sorting by one key after another.
Python and Java (objects) use Timsort; C++ std::sort is introsort; Rust's stable sort is a merge variant and unstable sort a pattern-defeating quicksort.
Everything smaller goes left, larger right; the pivot is then in its final place and both sides are sorted recursively.
Sorted input with a first-element pivot gives the quadratic case; median-of-three or random pivots avoid it, and introsort falls back to heapsort.
No bad inputs: the recursion depth and the work per level are fixed, which is why it suits linked lists and external sorting.

synapses.lead: The merge step is the whole trick
synapses.text: Merging two sorted sequences is linear; everything else is bookkeeping.
Real inputs often contain sorted runs; Timsort detects and extends them instead of ignoring the structure.
Java 7 switched object sorting to Timsort; a formal verification effort in 2015 found and fixed a bug in the run-stack invariant.
Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential because it recomputes the same values; caching makes it linear.
Knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance and shortest paths in DAGs are the standard DP problems.
Every recursive definition needs a case that does not recurse; forgetting it is the classic stack overflow.
When the recursive call is the last thing a function does, Scheme and some compilers reuse the frame; CPython deliberately does not.
Manual (C), automatic at runtime (GC in Java, Go, JavaScript; refcounting in CPython and Swift), or automatic at compile time (Rust ownership).
Forgetting to free leaks; freeing too early dangles. Each strategy trades one risk for another or for runtime cost.
A cache miss costs roughly a hundred times a hit, so layout and locality often matter more than algorithmic constants.
Each call pushes locals and a return address; recursion too deep overflows it.
Allocation involves an allocator, fragmentation and later deallocation; escape analysis lets some compilers keep heap-looking values on the stack.
A collector keeps anything reachable from roots (stack, globals); unreachable cycles are freed, which refcounting alone cannot do.
Most objects die young, so collecting the nursery often and the old generation rarely is cheaper than scanning everything.
Go's concurrent collector targets sub-millisecond pauses, trading some throughput for predictable latency.
CPython combines refcounts with a cycle collector; Swift's ARC inserts retain/release at compile time and uses weak references to break cycles.
Rust offers reference counting as an opt-in library type for shared ownership, atomic (Arc) when crossing threads.
Front end (lex, parse, check) produces an IR; the middle end optimises it; the back end emits machine code for a target.
CPython compiles to bytecode then interprets it; V8 interprets bytecode and JIT-compiles hot functions; the line is blurry.
Dead-code elimination and loop transformations are only valid if the program avoids undefined behaviour, which is where surprising C output comes from.
A context-free grammar describes valid programs; the parser produces an abstract syntax tree that every later phase walks.

synapses.lead: Recursive descent is what most hand-written parsers are
synapses.text: One function per grammar rule, calling each other; readable, fast, and used by Clang, Go and many others.

synapses.lead: Regular expressions are the lexer's theory
synapses.text: Tokens are regular languages; a lexer is a DFA built from them.

synapses.lead: One middle and back end for many languages
synapses.text: Front ends emit LLVM IR; LLVM optimises it and targets x86, ARM, RISC-V, WebAssembly and more.
LLVM and Clang are developed in the llvm/llvm-project monorepo.
A JIT guesses types from what it has seen, compiles fast code for that case, and falls back if a different type appears.
V8 runs Ignition (interpreter), then Sparkplug and TurboFan; HotSpot has C1 and C2; each tier spends more compile time for faster code.
Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built Unix at Bell Labs from 1969; Linus Torvalds released Linux in 1991 and it now runs most servers and every Android phone.
User programs ask the kernel for everything (files, sockets, memory, processes) through a narrow syscall interface.
The kernel is developed at torvalds/linux on GitHub as a mirror of the mailing-list workflow.
Processes cannot corrupt each other's memory; threads can, which is why shared-memory concurrency needs locks.
Runtimes can multiplex many lightweight tasks onto few OS threads; Go, Erlang and Java virtual threads all do this.
Memory is mapped in pages (commonly 4 KiB); the TLB caches translations, and a miss costs several memory accesses.
Allocation, file mapping and copy-on-write forks all rely on pages being mapped only when touched.
Link, internet (IP), transport (TCP/UDP) and application (HTTP, DNS) layers each solve one problem; the stack is the most successful abstraction in computing.
The network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite: Peter Deutsch's list from 1994 still describes most outages.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK establishes a connection and sequence numbers; closing takes four segments.

synapses.lead: Congestion control keeps the internet up
synapses.text: Slow start and AIMD (Van Jacobson, 1988) let TCP share links fairly without central coordination.

synapses.lead: UDP when you can afford loss
synapses.text: DNS, games and QUIC build on UDP to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking.
Each request stands alone; cookies, tokens and sessions are layered on top to remember who you are.
HTTP/1.1 reuses connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one connection, HTTP/3 moves to QUIC to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.
Fielding's 2000 dissertation described REST; most APIs are HTTP+JSON shaped loosely after it, with GraphQL and gRPC as alternatives.
E. F. Codd's "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" separated what data means from how it is stored.
The most deployed database engine, in every browser and phone; a single-file library with a famously thorough test suite.
The open-source relational workhorse, descended from Michael Stonebraker's POSTGRES project at Berkeley (1986).
An index is a sorted structure over one or more columns pointing at rows; range queries walk it in order.
Query plans show whether an index was used; a missing index on a join column is the most common performance bug.
Changes are logged before they are applied, so recovery can redo or undo them after a crash.
Read committed, repeatable read, serializable: weaker levels allow anomalies in exchange for concurrency; MVCC gives readers snapshots without blocking writers.

synapses.lead: Third normal form in one line
synapses.text: "Every non-key attribute must provide a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."
Analytics and caches duplicate data deliberately; the sin is doing it by accident.

synapses.lead: Code points are not bytes, or glyphs
synapses.text: A character may be several code points (combining marks, emoji sequences), and a code point several bytes; length is a question, not a number.
Ken Thompson sketched UTF-8 in a New Jersey diner in 1992; it is self-synchronising and sorts in code-point order.
NFC and NFD represent the same text differently; compare normalised strings or "é" will not equal "é".
0.1 and 0.2 are repeating binary fractions; rounding both and adding gives 0.30000000000000004.

synapses.lead: NaN is not equal to itself
synapses.text: NaN != NaN by specification, which breaks naive equality and sorting; use isnan.
Decimal or integer-cent types avoid binary rounding; floats are for measurements, not ledgers.
Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 after the kernel lost access to BitKeeper; it was self-hosting within days.
Each commit points to a tree of the whole project; identical files share the same hashed blob, so history is cheap.
A branch is a 41-byte file holding a commit hash; creating one is instant, which changed how people work.
Git is developed at git/git, mirrored from its mailing-list workflow.
Git compares both branch tips with their merge base; non-overlapping changes merge automatically.
Short-lived branches merged daily keep integration pain small; long-lived ones accumulate conflicts.
Rebase recreates each commit, so the result shares no identity with the original; force-pushing a shared branch strands collaborators.
git rebase -i squashes, reorders and rewords commits before review; the tool for turning a messy day into a readable story.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests; the shape keeps feedback quick.
Code that is hard to test is usually too coupled; TDD (Kent Beck) uses that pressure deliberately.
SQLite ships with test code that outweighs the engine many times over, including out-of-memory and crash tests.
Set up inputs, run the unit, check the outcome; one behaviour per test keeps failures readable.
Simple in-memory implementations are usually easier to maintain than mock frameworks that assert on call sequences.
QuickCheck for Haskell inspired ports everywhere; Hypothesis is the Python standard and integrates with pytest.
When a property fails, the framework searches for the smallest failing input, which is what makes the failure useful.
The fuzzer keeps inputs that reach new code paths and mutates them further, so it learns the input format without being told.
Google's service has fuzzed hundreds of open-source projects since 2016, reporting thousands of bugs.
gdb (1986) and lldb set breakpoints, step and inspect; print statements remain the most used debugger in the world.
Binary search over history finds the commit that introduced a bug in log₂(n) builds.
Explaining the problem aloud to an inanimate object works often enough to have a name.
Review quality drops sharply past a few hundred lines; split work into reviewable steps.
Formatters and linters remove the bikeshedding so humans can discuss design and correctness.
Static analysis and AI reviewers now comment on pull requests; treat their findings as leads to verify, not orders.
The practice comes from Extreme Programming: merging often means conflicts and breakages stay small.
Build, test, lint and deploy stages with dependencies form a DAG, scheduled by topological order.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking, feature, fix; a convention, not a guarantee.
package-lock.json, Cargo.lock and similar pin the whole resolved graph so builds are reproducible.
An eleven-line package was unpublished from npm and broke builds worldwide; the incident reshaped registry policy.

synapses.lead: Write programs that do one thing well
synapses.text: McIlroy's summary: do one thing, work together, handle text streams because that is a universal interface.
grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn is a data pipeline in one line; the shell is a lazy, streaming functional language in disguise.
Automaton-based engines (RE2, Rust regex) guarantee linear time; backtracking engines (PCRE, JavaScript) support backreferences but can blow up exponentially.
Nested quantifiers like (a+)+ against a non-matching string can take seconds; it is a real denial-of-service vector.
Ken Thompson's 1968 paper compiled regexes to machine code for the QED editor; the NFA construction bears his name.
Tutorials teach, how-tos solve, references describe, explanations illuminate; mixing them is why most docs feel wrong.
rustdoc, pydoc and JSDoc render comments into reference pages so documentation lives next to what it documents.
Knuth proposed (1984) writing programs as essays for humans from which code is extracted; notebooks are its descendants.
The seventh of her notes describes a step-by-step method for the Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers.
She wrote that the Engine might compose music if the relations of pitched sounds could be expressed; a prediction of general-purpose computing.
The 1936 paper introduced the Turing machine and showed no general procedure can decide whether a program halts.
Turing machines and Church's lambda calculus compute the same functions; the thesis that this captures all effective computation is named for both.
The ACM Turing Award, given since 1966, is named for him; several other neurons in this lobe received it.
A-0 translated symbolic code into machine code at a time when many believed computers could only do arithmetic.
Her team taped a moth found in a Harvard Mark II relay into the 1947 logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found"; the word was older, the story made it stick.
The algorithm named for him remains the standard for single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights.
His 1968 letter argued unrestricted goto made programs impossible to reason about; the title became a genre.
He introduced semaphores and the classic deadlock puzzle that still teaches concurrency.
The multi-volume work is the reference on algorithms and their analysis; Knuth pays a hexadecimal dollar for each error found.
"We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil" (1974).
He wrote TeX to typeset his books and proposed literate programming to write programs as literature.
Started on a spare PDP-7 in 1969; rewritten in C in 1973, which made it portable and set the model for every OS since.
Regular-expression construction, UTF-8, the Plan 9 system and Go all carry Thompson's hand.
Thompson's 1984 Turing lecture showed a compiler could insert a backdoor into itself; the founding text of supply-chain security.
CLU's clusters were abstract data types with hidden representation; the idea became classes, modules and interfaces everywhere.
Her 1987 keynote defined behavioural subtyping; it is the L in SOLID.
Lisp's conditional expressions, recursion and symbolic processing came from his 1960 paper on recursive functions of symbolic expressions.
He described automatic memory reclamation for Lisp in 1959; every managed runtime since inherits the idea.
Minutes before the Apollo 11 landing the computer raised overload alarms; the software shed low-priority tasks and kept flying, as designed.
She used the phrase to insist software deserved the same discipline as hardware; it was not a compliment at the time.

synapses.lead: Just a hobby, won't be big
synapses.text: His 1991 newsgroup announcement called Linux "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu".
Written in April 2005 over about two weeks; he named it after himself, he said, as "the stupid content tracker".
Named for Monty Python, not the snake; designed to be readable and to bridge the gap between shell scripting and C.
He stepped down in July 2018 and Python moved to an elected five-person Steering Council.
The language changed names twice before shipping in Netscape Navigator 2; the Java-like syntax was a management requirement.
